title: Zenith Pharmaceuticals — Private/VPC security architecture review
next_steps: Alex Chen to share VPC diagrams, hardened security group templates, and example egress policy (due 2025-08-28)
Priya Nambiar to run small-scale pilot behind customer's proxy and share test results (schedule week of 2025-09-01)
Sophie Laurent to circulate SOC 2 scope and ISO artifact list for review (due 2025-08-29)
action_items: Alex Chen: Send VPC architecture diagram and hardened firewall template (due 2025-08-28)
Priya Nambiar: Prepare sample NAT/proxy egress config and small-scale benchmark (due 2025-09-03)
David Kim: Share current NACL and egress gateway configuration (due 2025-08-25)
Marcus Li: Produce 1-page runbook for bastion + audit log collection (due 2025-08-30)
summary: Redwood team (AE + SE) walked the Zenith Pharmaceuticals engineering and security team through a proposed Private/VPC deployment topology, focusing on network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewall hardening, KMS integration for key management, and audit/logging requirements to meet SOC 2/ISO constraints. Customer raised questions about egress filtering, HSM vs KMS key residency, and log retention for compliance. Agreed next steps: share diagrams, run a confined pilot behind customer's proxy, and exchange compliance artifacts.
topics: Ingress and egress controls (NAT, proxy, firewall)
transcript:
Header: 2025-08-21 14:30 PDT — Duration ~70m. Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood SA); Maria Gonzales (Zenith CTO), David Kim (ZEN Head Security), Omar El-Amin (Network Eng), Sophie Laurent (Compliance), Aaron Vega (Platform Eng).

[00:00] Alex Chen: Okay we're recording, thanks everyone for joining. Quick intro — I'm Alex, AE on the account, with Priya and Marcus from the Redwood infra team. Um, Maria, do you want to kick off with your primary goals for today?

[00:15] Maria Gonzales: Yeah, thanks Alex. Broadly we need to understand how Redwood Private would sit inside our VPCs — our infosec team is most concerned about ingress/egress, auditability for SOC 2 and ISO, and whether keys can stay on-prem or in our KMS/HSM. We're not looking to expose PHI outside our network.

[00:40] Priya Nambiar: Great, that's exactly what we'll focus on. Today's agenda: network topology options, ingress patterns (bastion, LB), egress gating (nat, proxy), firewall rules and hardened SGs, key management, and logging + SIEM ingestion. We'll also surface a few tradeoffs — latency vs cost and degree of isolation.

[01:05] David Kim: Quick note — we need audit logs retained 7 years for a subset of datasets and we have a central Splunk cluster. Also SSO must be corporate SAML with RBAC mapping to AD groups.

[01:20] Marcus Li: Understood. At a high level, Redwood Private offers a customer-managed control plane option where the inference runtime runs inside your VPC. You can pin model versions and we support KMS integration. In terms of network, there are two canonical topologies: 1) Isolated subnets with private load balancers and a bastion for admin; 2) A more integrated pattern where the runtime is in dedicated subnets but routes through an internal egress proxy.

[01:55] Omar El-Amin: Can you expand on the egress proxy option — we currently force-all egress through our proxy and through a NAT gateway that logs flows. We cannot allow direct outbound to S3 in public internet.

[02:10] Priya Nambiar: Yes. For customers that require strict egress control we recommend two components: an Egress Proxy (forward proxy) that performs TLS interception or allowlist-based proxying, and a NAT gateway for non-proxy flows. Redwood's runtime can be configured to send all external calls via customer-supplied proxy endpoints. We also support an S3 VPC endpoint for model artifact pulls so those never hit the public internet.

[02:45] Maria Gonzales: How does that work for model downloads and updates? We need to ensure model weights or cache never egress to a non-approved storage region.

[03:00] Marcus Li: Two patterns: a) Host model artifacts in a customer-managed S3 bucket and provide an endpoint or role for Redwood runtime to fetch; b) Use an internal artifact mirror behind your ingress. If you host artifacts in your S3, you control region and encryption — Redwood can read via assumed-role with limited scope. That avoids public egress.

[03:25] David Kim: About keys — we use an HSM-backed KMS (on-prem). Can Redwood integrate with a customer HSM so that model keys never leave our control?

[03:40] Priya Nambiar: We support integration with customer KMS/HSM via a connector — runtime can be configured to call your KMS for envelope encryption and decryption. We also have an option to use Redwood-managed keys if customers prefer, but for regulated workloads we recommend customer KMS. Note there is additional latency on every startup call if the key handshake is synchronous; we suggest envelope keys cached in memory with tight TTL and audit hooks.

[04:20] Aaron Vega: When you say cache keys in memory, does that mean plaintext keys in process? That raises a red flag for us.

[04:30] Marcus Li: Good callout. We do not keep unwrapped long-lived keys on disk. The runtime maintains an in-memory envelope key which is used to decrypt session keys (short-lived). We can add support for PKCS#11 / HSM-backed sign operations so unwrapped material never touches the host if you require that. However, performance and engineering constraints differ per deployment.

[05:05] Sophie Laurent: For SOC 2 scoping, we need detailed access logs for administration actions and model access events. How granular are your audit logs and can they be forwarded to our SIEM?

[05:20] Priya Nambiar: Audit logs include: API request metadata, service account activity, admin role changes, model deploy/rollback events, and system-level runtime events. Logs can be shipped to your Splunk or SIEM over a secure forwarder or to an S3 bucket with lifecycle policies. We also provide optional request-level logging that can be scrubbed or redacted for PII.

[05:50] David Kim: Request-level logging must be opt-in and we need field-level redaction. Can you show how redaction works?

[06:05] Priya Nambiar: We have a redaction pipeline that masks specified JSON paths before logs leave the runtime. It's configured by policy and runs prior to export. I'll follow up with config snippets.

[06:30] Maria Gonzales: Network segmentation — we run a multi-tenant VPC with strict segmentation already. If Redwood sits in a shared VPC, how do you guarantee tenant separation?

[06:45] Marcus Li: For Private we recommend dedicated subnets and security groups per customer; you can also use separate VPCs and peer them to Redwood's managed network if desired. Within a single VPC we enforce strict SG and NACL templates. The runtime supports namespace isolation so cross-tenant data paths are prevented at the application layer as well.

[07:10] Omar El-Amin: We prefer separate VPCs for Prod and Non-Prod and would like to route prod traffic through a different egress gateway. Is that supported?

[07:20] Alex Chen: Absolutely — you can configure multiple egress endpoints by route table and tag worker pools accordingly. We'll include an example routing table in the diagram.

[07:40] [noise] 

[08:00] David Kim: Firewalling details — what minimal ports do you need open? Our security policy aims to deny by default.

[08:10] Priya Nambiar: Minimal inbound: port 22 for bastion (admin-only with cert auth), internal RPC ports between runtime nodes on ephemeral ranges (we'll provide the ranges), and the internal load balancer port for your application clients. Outbound: HTTPS to your KMS endpoint, S3/VPC endpoints, and the telemetry forwarder if you choose to enable remote logging. We'll provide a hardened security group template that denies everything else.

[08:45] Maria Gonzales: About telemetry — we do not want telemetry leaving our network unless it's to our SIEM. Can we fully disable Redwood-managed telemetry?

[08:55] Priya Nambiar: Yes. In Private mode you can disable Redwood-managed telemetry and point all logs/metrics to your collectors. The control plane can be customer-hosted as well for air-gapped scenarios. Note: disabling telemetry removes some automated diagnostics but runbooks can be exported for on-call.

[09:25] Sophie Laurent: Any certifications to share? We need evidence for ISO27001 controls and SOC 2 AICPA mapping.

[09:35] Alex Chen: We'll share our compliance pack — SOC 2 report redactions, control matrix mapping to ISO clauses, and a description of our PKI and audit logging. For Private/on-prem customers we include additional docs about deployment controls. I'll attach those to the follow-up.

[09:55] Maria Gonzales: One edge case — our legal team requires that metadata about requests (IP, timestamps, model id) remain in-region and under our control. How do you handle metadata?

[10:08] Marcus Li: Metadata can be stored in your region and forwarded to your logging endpoints. If you choose customer-managed control plane, all metadata stays inside your VPC. For hosted options we have region boundaries, but for Private/on-prem it's your tenancy.

[10:30] Omar El-Amin: Performance question — routing everything through our proxy will add latency. Can Redwood's batching and KV cache mitigate tail latency behind a proxy?

[10:45] Priya Nambiar: Yes, the runtime uses a local KV cache (we sometimes say KV cash in notes — that's a transcription quirk) and request batching at the GPU layer to hide upstream latency. We also support local artifact caches so model weights aren't pulled on every request. We'll share a configuration that reduces cache eviction and improves hit rate.

[11:20] David Kim: Are there hard dependencies on cloud provider-specific networking (e.g., AWS security group quirks)? We're hybrid — some workloads run in Azure on-prem equivalents.

[11:30] Marcus Li: The runtime is cloud-agnostic; networking primitives differ per cloud but the patterns are the same: private subnets, internal LB, NAT/egress proxy, VNet peering or VPC peering. We'll provide Azure-equivalent diagrams as well.

[11:55] [brief silence, typing] 

[12:10] Maria Gonzales: Let's talk about RBAC and SSO. We run Okta SAML and map groups to roles — can Redwood honor AD/Okta group mapping and enforce least privilege?

[12:20] Priya Nambiar: Yes. We support SAML and OIDC SSO with group-to-role mapping. Admin and operator roles are separate; service accounts can be created with short-lived tokens, and we integrate with your AD for user provisioning. We'll show a sample SAML assertion mapping.

[12:50] Aaron Vega: For service-to-service auth (runtime -> KMS, runtime -> artifact store), do you rely on IAM roles or TLS mutual auth?

[13:00] Marcus Li: Both are supported. We recommend cloud-native IAM where available (assume role), and mTLS for cross-datacenter links. For on-prem HSMs PKCS#11 and mutual TLS are common.

[13:25] David Kim: Logging retention — we need to be able to set retention by log type (ex: 7 years for audit, 90 days for metrics). Is that configurable?

[13:35] Priya Nambiar: Yes, retention is configurable in the log sink. If you ship to S3 you can set lifecycle rules; if you ship to Splunk you can configure indexes and TTLs there. We can also tag logs with sensitivity so that retention policies are enforced automatically.

[14:00] Maria Gonzales: Any specific firewall vendor gotchas? We run Palo Alto and a perimeter F5, and within our cloud we're using native security groups.

[14:12] Priya Nambiar: Palo Alto and F5 are common; you'll mostly need to allow the internal IP ranges for orchestration traffic and the control plane (if using managed control plane) — we'll provide an allowlist. For deep packet inspection you may need to add exceptions for mTLS between runtime nodes.

[14:40] Omar El-Amin: Can we do a smoke test where we put the runtime behind our firewall rules and try a set of sample calls?

[14:48] Alex Chen: Yes — that's the pilot we propose. Priya will coordinate a limited worker pool that lives in your non-prod VPC and run a small benchmark and redaction test.

[15:05] [crosstalk] Maria: Sounds good, thanks.

[15:20] Recap (Alex Chen): Action items — I'll send the VPC diagrams and hardened SG templates; Priya will prepare the egress/proxy sample and pilot schedule; Marcus will create the bastion/runbook doc; Sophie will send SOC2 scope. We agreed pilot target week of 2025-09-01 and initial artifact exchange by next week.

[15:45] David Kim: One last thing — can you show an example of audit log entries for a model deploy? We need the fields to map to our control matrix.

[15:55] Priya Nambiar: I'll attach a sample log schema in the follow-up email; it has request_id, actor, action, model_id, timestamp, and redaction flag.

[16:12] Maria Gonzales: Great, thanks. That covers it for us.

[16:20] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with materials. Meeting adjourned.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional transcription imperfections ("KV cash" for KV cache; "gnat gateway" instead of NAT gateway in the automated notes). Some speaker labels collapsed during the recording; timestamps approximate.

End of transcript.
